catalog_quote: 3.2 The phonological word may have from one to two phonetic syllables. The word must have one stressed syllable as nucleus and may optionally have one unstressed syllable preceding it as periphery. Stress in Kuay is predictable. That is ........ 3.2.1 ['c(c) v(c)] In one phonetic syllable word, stress is on that syllable. ['dxh] 'pot' ['cxxn] 'to be ripe' ['lxxw] 'button' ... 3.2.2 [c(c) v(c) 'c (c) v (c)] In two phonetic syllable word, stress is on the final syllable [tə'ŋəəl] 'to be bald' [lə'luŋ] 'to be loose' [kə'bxh] 'to blink (the eyes)' [kəŋ'hɔk] 'to cough' [səm'laap] 'rice seedlings' [tuŋ'saaj] 'rabbit' [mɔm'pruj] 'a bee' So there are two phonetic types of syllable patterns in Kuay (S = strong W = weak) a) S e.g. ['suar] 'to tell' ... WS e.g. [cə'ŋxxt] 'to be cool' [rəm'bɔɔŋ] 'fence' 3.3 The word proved phonemically to have only one syllable. (one word equals one syllable, except some words in section 3.3.2), since the [ə] vowel in initial unstressed phonetic syllable is predictable and can be defined phonemically as a reduced vowel transition between the first two elements. So the Stress pattern is only the strong stress on the main syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The Kuy phonological word is a monosyllable or a presyllable + main syllable; stress is predictable and always falls on the final (main) syllable, the optional presyllable being unstressed with a reduced schwa vowel. In compounds/reduplications (rhythm groups) primary stress falls on the last word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Within rhythm groups (compounds, reduplications) non-final words carry a weaker secondary stress and are shortened; primary stress on the last word (p.17). No word-internal secondary stress (words are at most disyllabic).
new_statements.exceptions: p.20: a few disyllables whose first syllable has a full (non-schwa) vowel (e.g. /puŋwaaj/ 'spider', /tuŋsaaj/ 'rabbit', /mompruj/ 'bee') are treated as exceptions to the one-word-one-syllable phonemicization, but they too are stressed on the final syllable (/cvc'c(c)v(c)/).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement within a hierarchical (breath group > rhythm group > phonological word) description; examples are citation forms from one speaker of Nong Bua Kuay, Suphanburi. Pitch is non-contrastive and predictable from syllable structure/register; presyllables always low pitch (p.23). Surin varieties described by Johnston 1976 (p.268) and Sa-Ard 1984 (p.20) agree: unstressed presyllable + stress-bearing major syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Yantreesingh 1980) describes the Kuay of Nong Bua village, Amphoe Mueang, Suphanburi Province (central Thailand) -- a displaced Kuy enclave; nearest Glottolog dialect node is Kuay [kuay1244] under Kuy [kuyy1240]. Two further first-hand sources saved held by the project describe core Surin varieties and agree: Johnston 1976 (Kuy Kuy dialect, Samrong Thap, Surin; PL C-43 p.268: major syllables carry stress, minor presyllables cannot) and Sa-Ard 1984 (Kuay of Ban Wan, Surin; p.20: first syllable of disyllables unstressed with neutral schwa). Note Glottolog's list for kuyy1240 also contains Dash 1981 'Structure of Kui: a tribal language of Orissa', which is the Dravidian Kui of India, a misattribution -- not this language.

new_statements.quote: A description of Kui phonology (and of orthography) is attached as separate document. A brief summary of the phonology is presented below. As is typical for Mon-Khmer languages, Kui has both monosyllabic and sesqui-syllabic syllable patterns. In the latter, the main syllable is prefixed with an unstressed minor syllable with a general structure of C1(C2)ɜ(N) or consists of a syllabic nasal (N). The main syllable is derived from the general structure C1(C2)V(C3). Kui has 22 consonant phonemes and a broad inventory of 35 vowel phonemes (representing both heavy and light register vowels).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (Yantreesingh 1980, Kuay of Suphanburi: 'In two phonetic syllable word, stress is on the final syllable') and as the statements held by the project from Sa-Ard 1984 (first syllable of disyllables unstressed, schwa nucleus) and Johnston 1976 (minor presyllable + major syllable). Bos adds the Cambodian Kuy Ntua dialect to the varieties for which the iambic/sesquisyllabic pattern is stated, with the minor-syllable template C1(C2)ɜ(N) ~ N.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kuy Ntua words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables; in a sesquisyllable the main (final) syllable carries the stress and is preceded by an unstressed minor syllable C1(C2)ɜ(N) or a syllabic nasal. Stress is thus non-contrastive and falls on the last (main) syllable of the phonological word. The sketch defers the full phonology to a separate (unnamed) phonology/orthography document; nothing else in the 97 pp. concerns word stress (only 'neutral intonation' for statements, p.72, and rising intonation on wh-questions, p.75).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the minor syllable may be a bare syllabic nasal (N); register (heavy/light) is a vowel property of the main syllable, not stress
new_statements.identity_note: Bos 2009 describes the Kuy Ntua dialect of Cambodia (language assistant from Promey village, Preah Vihear province; Kuy Ntua and Kuy Ntra are the two major Cambodian dialects per Markowski 2005), ISO kdt; the catalog record rests on Kuay of Suphanburi, Thailand (Yantreesingh 1980), with supporting statements for Surin varieties. All fall under glottocode kuyy1240.

sources.note: p.268 (Kuy Kuy dialect, Samrong Thap, Surin): 'Syllables in Kuy are of two principal types - major syllables, which may carry full sentence stress, and minor syllables, which may not. Minor syllables are often the presyllables of polysyllabic words.. With very few exceptions, polysyllabic words consist of a minor syllable consisting of /k t s ʔ/ + /a/ followed by a major syllable.' I.e. stress only on the (final) major syllable.
